Let’s talk about something that shapes so much of our lives, often in ways we don’t even realize—hunger.
Not just the kind that makes your stomach growl, but all the different forms it can take. This is Chapter 3: Hunger, Desire, and the Search for Control.
For some of us, hunger isn’t just about food—it’s a steady presence, quietly reminding us of everything that feels missing. Maybe it’s the ache for safety, the longing to be loved, or the deep desire to feel truly seen. Sure, food is the quickest way to fill that emptiness, but let’s be real—it’s rarely the whole story.
Think back to those teenage years. The world felt huge, unpredictable, even a little scary sometimes. When everything else seemed out of your hands, eating became something you could control. It felt like a secret rebellion against all the chaos. There was comfort in the little rituals: the way food tasted, the feeling of fullness. For a moment, things quieted down, and the hurt didn’t feel quite as sharp.
But the truth is, hunger goes way beyond what’s on your plate. It’s about wanting more from life—more safety, more love, more acceptance. It’s that wish to be held, to be cared for, to finally feel like you’re enough. And as the body changes and grows, it can send mixed signals. On one hand, it says—keep your distance. On the other, it’s almost begging, please notice me. Living with that contradiction? It isn’t easy, but it’s a reality for so many.
These complicated feelings ripple through our relationships, too. Getting close to someone starts to feel risky. Vulnerability? That can seem downright dangerous. When you’ve been hurt before, it’s hard to let your guard down, even with people who care. The body, marked by old wounds and shame, can start to feel undeserving of love. Yet, that longing—to be known, to be cherished—it never really goes away.
And what about all those attempts to change the body? Diets, exercise plans, sheer willpower—so much hope, followed by frustration when things don’t magically get better. We’re told that being thin will solve everything, but even on our “best” days, the hunger is still there. That’s when you start to realize—the real struggle isn’t just with the body. It’s with the pain hiding underneath.
Over time, there comes a quiet shift. You start to see that hunger isn’t the enemy. It’s part of being human—a sign that you have needs, that you still hope for something more. The real challenge? It’s not about getting rid of hunger, but learning to live with it. Finding ways to feed that emptiness without causing harm, and maybe, just maybe, showing yourself a little compassion along the way.
It’s not an instant fix. There will be setbacks and slow progress. But recognizing hunger for what it is—that’s a real beginning.
